title: Cedric Haywood, the self-taught arranger who taught him transposition
summary: Haywood taught Cobb transposition across a bed with the score, and rehearsed sections separately in different rooms until the band played from memory.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well now, he went to the coast and Lionel picked him up. Now you're still with Milt Larkin, right?
I was still with Milt Larkin. I left in Houston, from Houston.
Well, when -- just tell me a little bit about Cedric Haywood Seppin Hayworth. (PHONETIC).
Oh, you're talking about the champ, now. That was one of the greatest writers of all times, and a self made writer. And when he started writing his scores, he'd

put them in block chords, and you had to transport to find out what the instrumentation was. He was the one who taught me transposition. And he lived right across the street from the Harlem Grill where we played, and we laid across the bed with the score, and he would say, 'Now this goes for the baritone and this goes for the trumpet, and this goes for ...' and I would say, 'Well, I don't know the note; it was all concert.' And he would start to teach me transposition because he wanted to help him with concert arrangements.

And I said, "Gee willikers, this sure is fun". I had nothing else to do. And when we got the arrangements finished, I may have some wrong notes and he would correct me, and we're going to rehearsal. We weren't good readers, but we could spell a little bit. And he'd put the rhythm section on the bandstand, and he put the brass section in one rest room, and like men and women's rest rooms, and the reed section in another rest room, and we all separated, and he's running from one section to the other, to let them know what was going on.

Then he'd go back and let the rhythm section know; he would rehearse a whole section, but when he put it together, we had it together. But we got it by section, and we separated ourselves to do it. And we were so conscientious and he made us feel so good -- Cedrick -- but he didn't know, even himself, what he was doing during those days. Milton did. Milton was smart.
But when we put it together, we had it together, and

we would do memory rehearsal. We'd turn the sheet over. That's how much we rehearsed. We rehearsed so much that it photographed in your mind. Cedric And Cedrick would have a ball when you played his arrangements.
